source_text: Hanc ergo partem sententiae non solum a nostra definitione removisti, sed pro hac etiam intulisti tuam, quae prima fronte aliquid haberet invidiae, sed tamen discussa vanesceret. Posuisti enim nos dicere bonam a Deo bono conditam naturam, sed ita esse sanam, ut necessariam Christi non habeat medicinam. Intuere ergo, quanta penuria veritatis labores, qui et in ipsis verbis, quae dicuntur YYYY, furtum tam perspicuum facere non vereris; nam cum supra proposuisses: bonam naturam, subdidisti: ita esse sanam. Numquid YYYY boni sanum est? Certe cum dicimus bonum, nihil contra hoc proprie ponimus nisi malum; si autem causa poscit, ut sanum dicamus, ex adverso debile vel aegrum locamus ut, si sanum est, non utique debile, si debile, sanum non esse dicatur; cum autem dicimus: Bonum est hoc, a contrario eius non sani nomen, sed mali vocabulum sistimus. Tibi ergo dicendum fuit, quia definiremus nos bonam a Deo conditam naturam hominum, sed ita esse in parvulis bonam, ut institutionis suae nullum quaereret emendatorem, aut si ea, quae bona erant, alieno vocabulo, id est sanitatis indicare malebas, consonanti totum elocutione signasses. Nunc autem quasi murenula inter definitionum saxa prolaberis; cum enim te veritas compulisset, ut nos confitereris bonam hominum dicere naturam a Deo bono conditam atque in ea parte sententiae ut multam rationem, ita invidiam nullam videres, ad alia continuo verba migrasti subiciens: sed ita nos eam sanam defendere, ut medicinam Christi ei necessariam non esse credamus. Quodsi totum tu per imperitiam incurris, bardissimus, sin autem id astu facis, vaferrimus inveniris.
pass_a_gloss: This part therefore of the sentence you have not only removed from our definition, but for this you have also brought in yours, which on the first front would have something of envy, but nevertheless discussed would vanish. For you have placed us to say nature founded good by the good God, but so healthy that it does not have the necessary medicine of Christ. Look therefore with how great a poverty of truth you labor, who even in the very words which are called opposites do not fear to make so clear a theft; for when above you had proposed: good nature, you subjected: so to be healthy. Is healthy the opposite of good? Certainly when we say good, we place nothing against this properly except evil; but if the cause demands that we say healthy, from the adverse we locate the weak or sick so that, if it is healthy, it is not indeed weak, if weak, it is said not to be healthy; but when we say: This is good, we set from its contrary not the name of the healthy but the vocable of evil. To you therefore it was to be said that we define the nature of humans founded good by God, but so good in little ones that it would seek no emender of its institution, or if you preferred to indicate those things which were good by an alien vocable, that is of health, you would have signed the whole by a consonant elocution. Now however like a little eel you slide among the rocks of definitions; for when truth had compelled you that you confess us to say the nature of humans good, founded by the good God, and in that part of the sentence as much reason so no envy you were seeing, you migrated immediately to other words subjecting: but that we defend it so healthy that we believe the medicine of Christ not necessary to it. Which if you run into the whole through inexperience, you are found most dull; but if you do it by craft, most sly.

pass_b_english: You not only removed this part from our definition; in its place you inserted your own, which could arouse hostility at first glance but would disappear under examination. You wrote that we say nature was made good by the good God, but is so healthy that it does not need Christ’s medicine. See how short of truth you are, when you do not shrink from such obvious theft even in terms called opposites! Having first put ‘good nature,’ you then added ‘so healthy.’ Is ‘healthy’ the opposite of ‘good’?

Surely when we say ‘good,’ its proper opposite is nothing but ‘evil.’ If the subject requires us to say ‘healthy,’ we put ‘weak’ or ‘sick’ opposite it: if it is healthy, it is not weak; if weak, it is not healthy. But when we say ‘This is good,’ we identify its contrary with the word ‘evil,’ not with ‘healthy.’ You should therefore have said that we define human nature as created good by God, and as so good in infants that it needs no one to correct the way it was made. Or, if you preferred to indicate goodness by the different term ‘health,’ you should have marked the entire statement with consistent language.

Instead you slip like a little eel between the rocks of definitions. Truth forced you to admit that we call human nature good and made by the good God. Seeing much reason but no grounds for hostility in that part of the statement, you immediately shifted to other words, adding that we defend it as so healthy that we do not believe Christ’s medicine necessary for it. If you stumble into all this through ignorance, you prove utterly dull; if you do it by cunning, utterly crafty.

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
